title: Mona Leonarda
story: Leonardo painted the Mona Lisa in the early 1500s, and people still argue about who sat for it. This parody offers an answer: the sitter has the painter’s own beard.

title: Nail-Filing Slave
story: Michelangelo carved a group of struggling “captive” figures for Pope Julius II’s tomb; two of them are now in the Louvre. This imagined extra captive isn’t struggling at all. He is doing his nails.

title: The Manifestation of the Tomato (in Italy)
story: In Botticelli’s Birth of Venus, the goddess arrives from the sea on a giant shell. Here the shell delivers a tomato, a fruit that only reached Italy from the Americas in the 1500s.

title: The Poker Game
story: Sofonisba Anguissola was one of the few famous women painters of the Renaissance and became a court painter in Spain. She painted her sisters playing chess; this version swaps the chess for poker.

title: Really Sick Bacchus
story: Caravaggio once painted himself as Bacchus, the Roman god of wine, looking pale and unwell. This version pushes the joke much further.

title: Judith Shampooing Holofernes
story: Artemisia Gentileschi was one of the most successful painters of the Baroque, known for strong women from Bible stories, like Judith defeating the general Holofernes. In this version, Judith is washing his hair.

title: The Apoplectic Cavalier
story: Frans Hals’s Laughing Cavalier is famous for its smug grin. This “sequel” shows the moment after someone throws a glass of red wine at him.

title: The Turkey Dinner of Dr Tulp
story: Rembrandt’s group portrait of Dr Tulp shows a surgeon giving an anatomy lesson to a room of serious men. The parody swaps the lesson for a holiday turkey.

title: Haystacks
story: Monet painted the same haystacks again and again to study how light changes through the day and the seasons. This one adds a burning getaway car.

title: Mon déjeuner sur l’herbe
story: Berthe Morisot was the only woman in the first Impressionist exhibition in 1874. Manet’s famous Luncheon on the Grass showed dressed men picnicking with an undressed woman; this version flips who is wearing clothes.

title: Ear
story: Van Gogh had a troubled time in the south of France and famously injured his own ear. The parody shows the ear itself, wrapped up like a parcel.

title: Pastorales Tahitiennes
story: Gauguin left France for Tahiti looking for a simpler life, and he often saw himself as a misunderstood martyr. This painting puts that feeling right in the middle of the picture.

title: The Uncontrollable Giggle
story: Munch’s The Scream is the world’s most famous picture of panic. Here the same figure on the same bridge can’t stop laughing.

title: A Rose Is a Rose Is a Rose Is a Rose
story: Georgia O’Keeffe is known for giant close-up flowers and the deserts of New Mexico. The title borrows a famous line by the writer Gertrude Stein.

title: American Goths
story: Grant Wood’s American Gothic (1930) shows a stern farmer and a woman in front of their farmhouse. This parody imagines their great-grandchildren as goths.

title: Times Square Traffic Jam
story: Mondrian built his paintings from straight black lines and blocks of red, yellow and blue, and in New York he painted Broadway Boogie Woogie. This one turns his grid into gridlock.

title: Eating Gypsy
story: Henri Rousseau painted The Sleeping Gypsy, a lion standing over a sleeping traveller in the desert. This parody shows what the lion did next. Note: “Gypsy” is the old title of the painting, but many Roma people consider the word a slur.

title: Ceci est une cigarette
story: Magritte painted a pipe with the words “This is not a pipe”, because it is a picture of a pipe, not a real one. This parody says the opposite about a cigarette.

title: Le burger en fourrure
story: In 1936 Meret Oppenheim covered a teacup, saucer and spoon in fur, one of the best-known Surrealist objects ever made. Here it is a fur burger.

title: Self-Portrait with Beehive
story: Frida Kahlo painted dozens of self-portraits, many after a bus accident left her in lifelong pain. This one gives her a beehive hairdo, bees included.

title: Lady Gaga
story: Andy Warhol made brightly coloured, repeated portraits of celebrities like Marilyn Monroe. He died in 1987, a year after Lady Gaga was born. That is the joke.

title: I’m Just Transferring You.
story: Roy Lichtenstein painted giant comic-book panels, dots and all. This one imagines what he would make of a call-centre headset.

title: Untitled Film Still #5022
story: Cindy Sherman photographs herself playing characters in imaginary movie scenes. Here she plays Katniss from The Hunger Games.

title: You Just Stepped On My Toe
story: Barbara Kruger lays bold red-and-white slogans over photographs to make sharp points about society. This slogan is about something smaller: a sore toe.

title: Papa
story: Louise Bourgeois is famous for Maman, a giant spider sculpture over 9 metres tall. This imagined “Papa” is a giant tick.

title: All the Eternal Love I Have for Aubergines
story: Yayoi Kusama fills mirrored rooms with polka dots and her famous spotted pumpkins. This mirror room is full of spotted aubergines (eggplants).

title: How to Explain Pictures to a Dead Man
story: In 1965 Joseph Beuys spent hours explaining pictures to a dead hare, his head covered in honey and gold leaf. In this version the hare does the explaining.

title: Present
story: Christo and Jeanne-Claude wrapped enormous things in fabric, including the Reichstag building in Berlin. This piece wraps something as a gift.

title: The Artist Is Living in Your Home
story: In 2010 Marina Abramović sat silently at New York’s Museum of Modern Art for more than 700 hours while visitors took turns sitting across from her. This version moves her into your living room.

title: Little Big Pony
story: Jeff Koons is known for giant shiny balloon-dog sculptures and a huge puppy made of flowers. Here a toy pony becomes a beach-sized monument.

title: The Essential Saltiness of the Pickling Process in the Mind of the Consumer
story: Damien Hirst became famous for a shark preserved in a tank and for very long titles. This early piece preserves a pickle.

title: Every Pillow I Have Ever Slept With
story: Tracey Emin makes very personal art; one famous piece is simply her own unmade bed. This one is a tower of her old pillows.

title: My Homepage
story: Jean-Michel Basquiat moved from New York street graffiti to top galleries before his death in 1988, often painting crowns and raw, angry faces. This imagines him designing a social media page.

title: Self-Portrait
story: Nobody publicly knows who Banksy is. This “self-portrait” still doesn’t tell you.

title: Pop Plane
story: Keith Haring’s bold dancing figures appeared in New York subway stations and murals, and in 1986 he opened his Pop Shop. Here his figures cover a jet plane.

title: Don’t Mess with Missy
story: Miss Van, a street artist from Toulouse, France, paints confident cartoon “dolls” on city walls. This doll is standing up for herself.
